Document vectors are precomputed, leaving only a cheap comparison per query
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Because document embeddings are computed once at index time, each query needs only one encoding pass plus a dot product against the stored vectors. A model that re-reads the query and document together would instead require a full pass for every document.

05 - Semantic Search.question: When indexing long documents for a dense bi-encoder, a team splits them into much smaller passages than they use for their keyword index. Why do the dense vectors benefit from the smaller passages?
options: A long passage is squeezed into one vector, blurring relevant content
A long passage exceeds the dot-product limit of the vector index
Shorter passages let the keyword index and the dense index share one score
Shorter passages are required for cosine similarity to stay below one
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: A bi-encoder compresses an entire passage into a single fixed vector. A long passage mixes many topics, so relevant content gets diluted by unrelated text. A keyword index scores individual terms, so it tolerates much larger chunks.

05 - Semantic Search.question: Both an early latent-topic method and a modern dense retriever produce documents as dense vectors rather than sparse term lists. Compared with a classical keyword system, what cost do both pay at search time?
options: Each query must be re-encoded once for every document in the collection
Each query must be compared against every document, without index pruning
Each document must be re-indexed whenever a new query arrives
Each query returns fewer documents than the keyword system allows
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Dense vectors are not sparse, so the inverted-index pruning tricks (skip pointers, early termination) do not apply. Both approaches must in principle compare the query against every stored document vector, which is why brute-force dense search costs one dot product per document.

05 - Semantic Search.question: In a latent-topic retrieval model, how is a new search query placed into the same low-dimensional space as the stored documents?
options: It is matched directly in the original high-dimensional term space
It is projected with the mapping that places documents there
It is re-trained into the model by recomputing the full factorisation
It is averaged from the vectors of the documents it most resembles
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: A query is treated as a short document and folded into the latent space with the same transformation applied to documents. This avoids recomputing the decomposition for every query.

05 - Semantic Search.question: Two word-embedding models are tested on a rare, misspelled term that neither saw during training. The first returns nothing useful; the second still produces a sensible vector. What ability explains the second model's behaviour?
options: It builds the term's vector from smaller character fragments it has seen
It falls back to the single most frequent word in its vocabulary
It looks the term up in an external spelling-correction dictionary
It averages the vectors of every word in the training corpus
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: A sub-word model composes a word's vector from character n-gram vectors. Because those fragments recur across many known words, an unseen or misspelled term can still be assembled into a meaningful vector, while a pure word-level model has no entry for it.

05 - Semantic Search.question: A retrieval model keeps a separate vector per document token and matches each query token to its best document token, rather than compressing each document into one vector. This costs more storage and more comparisons. What retrieval benefit justifies that cost?
options: It removes the need to encode documents before queries arrive
It captures fine-grained semantic matches a single vector would blur
It guarantees exact-string matches such as identifiers and codes
It shrinks each document to fewer dimensions than a keyword index
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Compressing a whole passage into one vector loses detail. Keeping a vector per token lets each query token find its best-matching document token, capturing fine-grained semantic alignment close to a cross-encoder's quality, while documents can still be encoded ahead of time. The extra storage and comparison cost is the price paid for that quality.

05 - Semantic Search.question: To save storage and speed up search, a team compresses every embedding down to a single bit per dimension. This strong approximation introduces ranking errors. How is that error typically compensated in the pipeline?
options: Increase the single-bit vectors to two bits per dimension
Discard the full-precision vectors once the bits are computed
Encode each query jointly with every document in the collection
Rescore the top candidates with the full-precision vectors afterwards
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: The compressed vectors act as a coarse first-stage filter. Because the approximation drops precision, the surviving top candidates are rescored with the full-precision embeddings to recover ranking quality. This is the same two-stage idea used with Matryoshka embeddings, where a truncated prefix filters and the full vector reranks; a cross-encoder reranker plays the same corrective role.

05 - Semantic Search.question: A search team finds that their keyword engine misses paraphrased queries, while their dense engine mishandles exact identifiers like serial numbers. They want one system that handles both query types well. Which design most directly achieves this?
options: Replace both engines with a single larger dense embedding model
Increase the number of latent dimensions in the dense engine
Apply a cross-encoder to the keyword engine's results only
Run both engines in parallel and fuse their result lists
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: A hybrid pipeline runs sparse (keyword) and dense retrieval in parallel and merges the two lists, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. Sparse retrieval captures exact identifiers and rare terms; dense retrieval captures paraphrases. A bigger model or more dimensions still struggles with exact strings, and reranking the keyword results alone cannot recover documents the keyword engine never retrieved.

05 - Semantic Search.question: An embedding model is trained so that the first part of each vector is already useful on its own. A team uses the short prefix to scan the whole collection quickly, then the full vector to re-rank the survivors. What advantage does this give over keeping two separate models?
options: The short prefix captures more detail than the full-length vector
The full vector can be discarded once the prefix is computed
Both stages share one model, needing no extra encoder
The prefix and full vector must be stored in two different indexes
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Because truncated prefixes of a Matryoshka embedding are themselves usable, the cheap first stage and the precise rerank stage come from a single model and a single stored vector. No separate small-model index or extra encoder is required.

05 - Semantic Search.question: After training on a large corpus, a word-vector space lets you take the vector for a capital city, subtract its country, add a different country, and land near that country's capital. What property of the embeddings does this illustrate?
options: Relational patterns are encoded as consistent directions in the space
Each word vector stores an explicit list of its dictionary senses
The vectors are sorted alphabetically along one of the axes
Every city shares an identical vector with its own country
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Training on co-occurrence produces a space where relationships such as country-to-capital appear as roughly constant offset directions. Vector arithmetic can therefore move from one word to a related one, which is why analogies work.

05 - Semantic Search.question: An engineer takes a pre-trained masked-language transformer, mean-pools its token outputs into one vector per sentence, and uses cosine similarity for retrieval. The results are worse than averaging simple static word vectors. Why does the raw transformer disappoint here?
options: Its token outputs are identical for every sentence it processes
Mean pooling cannot be applied to transformer outputs at all
Cosine similarity is undefined for vectors above a certain dimension
Its token states were tuned for pre-training, not sentence comparison
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: A masked-language model's internal states are shaped by its pre-training objectives (predicting masked tokens and sentence adjacency), not by making whole-sentence vectors comparable by cosine. Without fine-tuning on sentence pairs, as Sentence-BERT does, pooling those states compares poorly, sometimes worse than averaging static word vectors.

05 - Semantic Search.question: When choosing an embedding model, a team considers moving from a 384-dimensional model to a 4096-dimensional one. What is the main downside of the higher-dimensional choice?
options: It can only be used for multilingual collections
It cannot be combined with a keyword index
It raises storage and search cost per vector
It prevents any form of quantization later
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Higher-dimensional embeddings can capture more nuance, but every stored vector takes more space and every comparison does more arithmetic, raising both storage and query cost. The dimension choice is a quality-versus-cost tradeoff.

05 - Semantic Search.question: Averaging static word vectors gives the sentences "a dog bit the man" and "the man bit a dog" the same representation. A trained sentence encoder distinguishes them. What underlies this improvement?
options: The encoder lets tokens interact, so order and structure matter
The encoder uses a larger vocabulary than the word-vector model
The encoder stores each sentence as a list of separate word vectors
The encoder removes stop words before building the sentence vector
05 - Semantic Search.explanation: Averaging word vectors ignores order, so two sentences with the same words collapse to one vector. A transformer-based sentence encoder lets tokens attend to each other, so word order and syntactic structure change the resulting vector, letting it tell the two sentences apart.

06 - Vector Search.question: A vector index stores document embeddings that were all scaled to unit length before indexing. At query time, the system ranks the documents by their dot product with the raw query embedding, which has a length of 3.7. How does this ranking compare with a ranking by cosine similarity?
options: It is the same ranking; only the scores are scaled differently
It favors documents whose length is closest to the query length
It is distorted unless the query is also scaled to unit length
It matches cosine only if the query length is below 1.0
06 - Vector Search.explanation: Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both vector lengths. All stored vectors have length 1, so only the query length remains as a divisor. That length is the same for every document, so it scales all scores of the query by the same factor and leaves the order unchanged. Normalizing the query is only needed when scores must be comparable across queries.

06 - Vector Search.question: An inverted-file index splits 50 million vectors into 2,000 clusters. When it probes 40 clusters per query, recall@10 measured against exact search is 0.90. The team doubles the number of probed clusters to 80. What is the most likely effect?
options: Throughput roughly halves while recall improves only slightly
Throughput stays stable while recall rises close to a perfect 1.0
Recall improves strongly while the share of data read stays fixed
Recall drops because more clusters add distant, irrelevant vectors
06 - Vector Search.explanation: The search cost grows linearly with the number of probed clusters, so twice the probes means about twice the work and half the throughput. Each additional cluster recovers fewer missed neighbors than the one before, because most true neighbors already sit in the nearest clusters. Recall cannot drop, because recall compares against the exact top 10 and more probes only add candidates.

06 - Vector Search.question: A search engine combines a vector clause and a keyword clause in one Boolean query, and the final score is the sum of the clause scores. The vector clause returns a cosine-based score between 0 and 1. The keyword clause returns BM25 scores. A user's query contains a person's name that appears in only a handful of documents. What happens to the final ranking?
options: Documents with the name dominate, whatever their vector similarity
Both clauses contribute equally, since each score has the same range
The vector clause dominates, since it scores every document it sees
Documents with the name drop lower, since rare terms add noise to scores
06 - Vector Search.explanation: A rare name has a high IDF, so its BM25 contribution can reach several points. The vector clause adds at most 1. When the scores are added, matching the name outweighs any difference in vector similarity. Boosts that weight the clauses, or rank fusion such as RRF, which uses only ranks, avoid this imbalance.

06 - Vector Search.question: A distributed search engine splits a collection across eight shards. Each shard holds its own HNSW graph and returns its 10 best matches for a query. A coordinating node then merges the eight lists into a global top 10. Compared with exact search over the full collection, where can the global result go wrong?
options: Only inside the shards, where each graph search is approximate
Only in the merge, which can drop matches ranked 11th in a shard
In both steps, since each shard compares only part of the data
Nowhere, since searching eight smaller graphs makes them exact
06 - Vector Search.explanation: Every document in the global top 10 is also among the top 10 of its own shard, because at most ten documents in the collection, and therefore in any one shard, can rank above it. Merging the per-shard lists therefore cannot lose a global top-10 match. Any error comes from the HNSW search inside each shard, which may miss true neighbors. The price of sharding is cost, not accuracy: every query must visit every shard.

06 - Vector Search.question: A system filters during an inverted-file search. A bitmap marks the admitted documents, and the scan of the probed clusters skips all others. For one query, the filter admits only 2,000 of 500 million vectors. How should the system answer this query?
options: Skip the index and compare the query exactly with the admitted vectors
Keep the usual number of probed clusters, since the bitmap check is cheap
Run the search unfiltered and remove non-admitted results afterwards
Probe fewer clusters than usual, since fewer vectors need to be checked
06 - Vector Search.explanation: With such a selective filter, the probed clusters contain only a few admitted vectors, and the best admitted matches probably sit in clusters that were not probed. An exact scan over 2,000 vectors is cheap and returns the exact top results. Post-filtering would be worse still: almost none of the unfiltered results would pass the filter.

06 - Vector Search.question: An audio search system describes each track by 20 spectral values, each between 0 and 1, plus the track's tempo in beats per minute, which ranges from 60 to 180. Tracks are compared with Euclidean distance on these raw values. What happens to the search results?
options: Tracks are matched almost only by how close their tempos are
Tracks are matched mostly by spectrum, as it has more dimensions
Tracks are matched by both parts equally, as each is one feature
Tracks cannot be compared, as the two parts use different units
06 - Vector Search.explanation: A tempo difference of 20 beats per minute outweighs any possible difference across all 20 spectral values combined, so the distance effectively compares tempo only. Gaussian normalization fixes this: each dimension is shifted by its mean and divided by its standard deviation, both estimated once from the collection. Every dimension then contributes in proportion to how much it actually varies.

06 - Vector Search.question: A Voronoi diagram precomputes the nearest neighbor for every possible query by dividing the space into one cell per stored point. Why is it not used as an index for 50-dimensional feature vectors?
options: The cell structure grows explosively with the number of dimensions
The cells only give correct answers for Euclidean distance measures
The cells must be recomputed from scratch for every incoming query
The cells return approximate answers instead of the exact neighbor
06 - Vector Search.explanation: In two dimensions, the diagram's size grows in proportion to the number of points. In higher dimensions, its worst-case size grows with a power of the number of points that rises with the dimension. Finding the query's cell then becomes as hard as the search it was meant to replace. Voronoi diagrams also exist for other distance measures, and their answers are exact.

06 - Vector Search.question: A team must search 2 billion embeddings. The full vectors take 6 TB, while the servers have 512 GB of main memory in total. The team needs a recall@10 of about 0.9. Which index design fits best?
options: An inverted file over compact codes held entirely in main memory
An HNSW graph over all vectors, with the full vectors kept on disk
An exact tree index over all vectors, with the leaves kept on disk
A full scan over the original vectors, run in parallel from disk
06 - Vector Search.explanation: The vectors must shrink by about a factor of 12 to fit into 512 GB, and product-quantization codes compress them by a factor of 16 to 64. The codes therefore fit into main memory, and the inverted file scans only a few lists per query, which is enough for a recall of about 0.9. HNSW jumps between arbitrary nodes and needs the full vectors in main memory. Exact trees read almost all leaves in high dimensions, and a full scan of 6 TB per query is far too slow.

06 - Vector Search.question: An online shop ranks products with an HNSW index. A query asks for the 10 most similar products that are in stock. The index returns its 50 best candidates, and the in-stock condition is checked only afterwards. Only 4% of all products are in stock. What does the user most likely see?
options: About two products, far fewer than the ten that were requested
Ten products, since the index keeps searching until ten pass
No products, since conditions cannot be applied after a search
Ten products, but in a less accurate order than without a filter
06 - Vector Search.explanation: This is post-filtering. Of the 50 candidates, about 4%, or two products, pass the in-stock check, even though many matching products exist further down the ranking. Fetching more candidates helps only if the selectivity is guessed correctly. A more robust approach treats the index as a stream of candidates and keeps consuming it until ten products pass.

06 - Vector Search.question: One system reports each match as a cosine distance (one minus the cosine) and sorts by the smallest value. Another system reports (1 + cosine) / 2 and sorts by the largest value. Both use the same embeddings and exact search. How do their result orders compare?
options: Both give the same order; one sorts ascending, the other descending
The orders differ, since one is a distance and the other a similarity
The orders differ, since only the second value stays between 0 and 1
Both give the same order, but only if the query vector has unit length
06 - Vector Search.explanation: Both values are simple functions of the cosine. The cosine distance falls as the cosine rises, and (1 + cosine) / 2 rises with it. Sorting the first ascending and the second descending therefore gives the same order. Turning a score into a distance, or rescaling it, changes only the direction and scale of the values, never the ranking.

06 - Vector Search.question: A tree index and an inverted file both divide the space into regions. For the same query, the tree opens 9 regions and returns the exact nearest neighbor. The inverted file opens 3 regions and misses it. What explains the difference?
options: The tree proves no closer point exists elsewhere; the file skips this check
The tree uses tighter regions, so its first region always holds the answer
The file's clusters overlap, so its distance computations become inaccurate
The file compares compressed codes, so the neighbor's distance came out wrong
06 - Vector Search.explanation: An exact tree search keeps opening regions until no unopened region could hold a closer point. That proof is why it opened 9 regions. The inverted file probes only a fixed number of the nearest clusters and accepts that a neighbor just across a boundary may sit in an unprobed cluster. In high dimensions, the proof forces the tree to open almost every region, which is why approximate methods drop it.

06 - Vector Search.question: A map service stores points of interest in an R-tree and inserts many new points over a year. The tree stays balanced, with all leaves at the same depth, yet queries become steadily slower. What is the most likely cause?
options: Overlapping rectangles force queries to follow several branches
Leaves grow beyond their capacity, so each read takes much longer
The tree loses balance, so some paths grow much longer than others
Deleted points leave empty rectangles that queries must still visit
06 - Vector Search.explanation: When a new point falls into the overlap of two rectangles, the insertion must pick one of them, and a poor choice inflates a rectangle. Inflated rectangles overlap their neighbors even more. Every query that reaches an overlapping region must follow several branches, so the tree loses the single root-to-leaf path that makes a B-tree fast. Node splits keep the tree balanced and the leaves within capacity.

06 - Vector Search.question: A greedy search on a navigable small-world graph moves from node to node, always to the linked neighbor closest to the query. It stops at a node where no linked neighbor is closer to the query. Yet the collection contains a vector that is closer. How can this happen?
options: The closer vector is reachable only via nodes farther from the query
The closer vector was stored in a higher layer that the search skipped
The closer vector has no links, as every node links only to its friends
The closer vector lies in a different cluster that was never probed
06 - Vector Search.explanation: The stopping node is a local minimum of the distance on the graph, not necessarily the global one. The path to the closer vector first leads through nodes that are farther from the query, and a purely greedy search never takes such a step. Keeping a list of the best ef_search candidates and expanding all of them lets the search continue past local minima. In HNSW, every vector is on the base layer and has links.

06 - Vector Search.question: A database searches 1,024-dimensional embeddings through an index on one-bit codes that keep only the sign of each component. An inner query retrieves the 100 best candidates by Hamming distance. An outer query reorders them by cosine distance on the full vectors and returns the top 10. Why is this top 10 much better than the first 10 candidates by Hamming distance?
options: Codes find the right region but cannot order close matches well
Codes skip the filter step, so reranking removes non-matching rows
Codes favor long vectors, and the full vectors correct this length bias
Codes are compared by Hamming distance, which reverses the order
06 - Vector Search.explanation: One-bit codes approximate the angle between vectors coarsely. The Hamming distance takes only a limited number of values, so many candidates tie, and close matches within a cluster are hard to tell apart. The codes reliably bring the good matches into the 100 candidates, and the exact comparison on the full vectors then puts them in the right order.

06 - Vector Search.question: A team has an R-tree whose split and insertion rules were designed for Euclidean distance. They reuse it to answer best-match queries under the dot product, changing only the function that bounds the score of each rectangle. What happens?
options: Results stay exact, but the search may open many more nodes
Results become approximate, since rectangles fit only Euclidean
Results stay exact and the search costs the same as for Euclidean
Results become wrong, since the dot product is not a valid metric
06 - Vector Search.explanation: The best-first search only needs a bound for each region that never promises less than the region could deliver. Nested rectangles keep this property under the dot product, so the results stay exact. The split and insertion rules, however, group vectors that are close in Euclidean distance, not vectors that score similarly under the dot product, so the search may have to open many more nodes. Only metric trees that prune with the triangle inequality cannot use the dot product directly.

06 - Vector Search.question: Spatial indexes were first designed for range queries, such as finding all shops within 2 km of a location. Why is a nearest-neighbor query harder for the same index?
options: The search does not know in advance how far away its answer lies
The search must compare the query with every point in the collection
The search can only use rectangles and not circles as query regions
The search returns a single point, which needs a deeper tree descent
06 - Vector Search.explanation: A range query knows its region before the search starts, so the index only has to find the parts of the space that overlap it. A nearest-neighbor query must first find a candidate and then prove that no other point is closer. If the query lies near the edge of a region, the closest point may sit in a neighboring region, so the search often follows more than one path.

06 - Vector Search.question: A product-quantization index splits every vector into sub-vectors and stores each one as the number of its nearest codebook center. For each query, it first computes the distance from every query sub-vector to every center of the matching codebook. What does scoring one stored vector then cost?
options: One table look-up per code, added up over all of its sub-vectors
One full distance computation between the query and the stored vector
One decoding of the vector back to floats, then an exact comparison
One comparison of the query against the vector's nearest cluster center
06 - Vector Search.explanation: The per-query tables already hold the distance between each query sub-vector and every center that a code can refer to. The approximate distance to a stored vector is the sum of one table entry per code. No multiplication over the original dimensions is needed, and the vector is never decoded. The tables are small enough to fit into the processor cache, which keeps the look-ups fast.

06 - Vector Search.question: A hybrid search fuses a vector ranking and a BM25 ranking with reciprocal rank fusion. In the vector ranking, the first document has a cosine of 0.92, the second 0.91, and the third 0.40. How does the fusion treat this gap in scores?
options: It ignores the gap, since only the ranks 1, 2, and 3 enter the fusion
It widens the gap, since the reciprocal of a low score grows very large
It keeps the gap, since each score is divided by the same constant first
It removes the third document, since its score is below a fixed cutoff
06 - Vector Search.explanation: Reciprocal rank fusion uses only the position of each document in each ranking. The third document receives the same contribution whether its cosine is 0.90 or 0.40. This is why it can fuse cosine scores and BM25 scores without calibrating them against each other. The price is lost information: a fusion that normalizes and weights the scores keeps the gap, but it requires choosing a normalization and the weights.

06 - Vector Search.question: A filtered vector search keeps pulling candidates from the index in order of increasing distance until ten of them pass the filter. Which property makes an HNSW index suit this approach well?
options: Its search already keeps a queue that can be extended further out
Its graph stores the filter values next to each node's list of links
Its layers sort all vectors by distance to the query before searching
Its links connect each vector to all vectors that pass the same filter
06 - Vector Search.explanation: Pulling candidates in order of distance is the same idea as the best-first nearest-neighbor search over trees, which returns its neighbors one by one from a priority queue. An HNSW search already maintains a queue of candidates. Continuing the search extends this queue into regions farther from the query, until enough candidates pass the filter. The graph itself knows nothing about the metadata.

06 - Vector Search.question: In 200 dimensions, an exact tree index ends up reading almost all of its leaves for every query. An alternative exact method first scans a compact code of a few bits per dimension for every vector. From each code, it derives a lower and an upper bound on the distance, and it reads in full only the vectors that could still be among the top results. Why is this alternative faster than the tree?
options: It reads much less data in one sequential pass over the codes
It skips most clusters far from the query and accepts a few misses
It never reads a full vector, since the codes alone decide the result
It reads the full vectors in tree order, which avoids repeated reads
06 - Vector Search.explanation: If every leaf must be read anyway, the only remaining gain is to make reading cheaper. The codes take 4 to 8 times less space than the full vectors, and scanning them is a sequential read without the random accesses of a tree. The bounds discard almost all vectors, so only a few candidates are read in full and compared exactly, and the result remains exact.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A RAG system runs BM25 over parent chunks of about 2,000 tokens and dense retrieval over small child chunks of about 200 tokens. Each child belongs to exactly one parent. The two result lists are to be merged with reciprocal rank fusion. What must happen before fusion can produce a sensible ranking?
options: Map each dense hit to its parent and merge repeated parents into one entry
Normalize BM25 and cosine scores to a common range so they can be added
Cut both result lists to the same length so each engine contributes equally
Drop every parent chunk that appears in only one of the two result lists
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Rank fusion assumes that both lists rank the same kind of item. Dense hits are child chunks, so each one must first be resolved to its parent. Several children often belong to the same parent, so these duplicates are collapsed into one entry that keeps its best rank or a combined score. RRF works on ranks, not scores, so score normalization is not needed. Truncating the lists or dropping single-list items throws away the complementary hits that hybrid retrieval exists to find.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A team must choose between two chunking strategies for a RAG system over technical manuals. Strategy X yields chunks that cluster tightly around 950 characters. Strategy Y yields chunks spread between 300 and 1,000 characters. How should the team decide?
options: Prefer X, whose chunk sizes are the most uniform
Prefer Y, whose chunk sizes best follow the content
Prefer the strategy that produces the larger number of chunks
Compare answer recall at k on a set of test questions
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: A size histogram cannot show whether chunk boundaries line up with answers. The dependable test holds the rest of the pipeline fixed, runs both strategies on questions with known answers, and checks whether the top k retrieved chunks contain each answer. Uniform or content-shaped sizes are useful hints, but neither proves better retrieval, and more chunks do not imply higher recall.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A hospital builds a RAG assistant that answers dosage questions from approved drug leaflets. An invented detail in an answer could harm a patient. Which result-generation form fits, and what does the team give up?
options: A reader; it cannot merge two partial answers into one
A generator; it cannot cite the leaflet it drew from
A synthesizer; it cannot answer within a single retrieval pass
A generator; it cannot return the exact wording of the leaflet
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: In high-risk settings, the reader's inability to add anything is a feature: it returns only a span that is literally present in the passage. The price is rigidity, because it cannot combine two half-answers or rephrase an awkward one. A generator can cite and can quote, but it can also invent details. A synthesizer adds iteration and is the hardest form to keep honest.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A RAG system splits legal contracts into fixed-size chunks of 800 characters without overlap. On questions about termination clauses, context recall is low. The team replaces the reranker with a stronger cross-encoder and the generator with a larger model. What is the likely effect on these questions?
options: Little change, since split clauses still never arrive whole
Higher recall, since the cross-encoder reads query and chunk together
Higher correctness, since a larger model can fill in the missing text
Lower precision, since the stronger reranker keeps more candidates
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Fixed-size boundaries fall wherever the character count runs out, so a clause can be cut across two chunks and no single chunk contains it. A reranker only reorders what retrieval returned, so it cannot recover text that no candidate holds whole. A larger generator that fills the gap would be inventing, which lowers faithfulness. The fix belongs in chunking: overlap, sentence or structural boundaries, or hierarchical chunks.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A company assistant receives three kinds of questions: general definitions such as "what is an API", counts such as "how many tickets were opened yesterday", and questions about internal policies that change every month. Which design fits best?
options: An agent routing each question to memory, the database, or policy search
One fixed RAG pipeline over all company documents, used for every question
A model fine-tuned every month on the policies and the ticket records
Long-context prompts holding all policies and the full ticket table
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Each kind of question has a different best tool. Stable definitions are already known to the model, counts need an exact database query rather than retrieval over text, and changing policies need retrieval from a fresh index. An agent can decide per query. A single RAG pipeline adds cost and only approximates the counts, fine-tuning goes stale and is the wrong tool for supplying facts, and putting everything in the prompt does not scale to a full ticket table.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: To save tokens, a RAG system drops all passage metadata after reranking and passes only the plain text to the generator. Once the answer is written, it asks the model to add a source URL for each claim. What is the main risk?
options: Cited sources may be made up, since no link to the used passages exists
Answers become less fluent, since the model must also write the URLs
Retrieval recall drops, since passages without metadata cannot be ranked
Latency doubles, since each cited claim triggers a second retrieval pass
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: A trustworthy citation needs an auditable link between the answer and the passages that produced it. This link is kept by carrying passage IDs, sources, and URLs through every stage. Without that metadata, the model can only guess or invent sources, which looks checkable but is not. Ranking happened before the metadata was dropped, and adding URLs does not trigger new retrieval.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: An agent loop has no limit on the number of steps. One of its tools keeps returning an error, and the agent keeps retrying it. What happens?
options: The loop never ends and keeps spending tokens on new calls
The output guardrail ends the loop after the first failure
The model switches to its fallback tool after a fixed timeout
The framework returns the last good answer to the user
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: The loop ends only when the model replies without a tool call or when an iteration budget is reached. Without a budget, a confused agent can retry forever, and every pass costs another model call. Output guardrails check the final answer, not repeated tool failures. A fallback only happens if the model chooses it, and nothing returns an answer automatically.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A RAG answer contains four claims, and all four are factually true. The retrieved context supports three of them. The model took the fourth from its own memory. How do faithfulness and correctness come out?
options: Faithfulness is 0.75; correctness stays unaffected
Faithfulness is 1; correctness stays unaffected
Faithfulness is 0.75; correctness also drops to 0.75
Faithfulness is 1; correctness drops to 0.75
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Faithfulness is the fraction of the answer's claims that the retrieved context supports, so it is 3/4. It measures grounding, not truth: a true claim from memory still lowers it, because the next claim from memory could just as easily be wrong. Correctness is judged against a reference, and all four claims are right, so it is not lowered.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A system indexes small chunks and also stores the parent section of each chunk. It receives two queries: "When was the company founded?" and "Summarize our travel policy." Which combination fits these two queries, in order?
options: A reader on the top chunk; a generator on the parent section
A generator on the parent section; a reader on the top chunk
A reader on the parent section; a synthesizer on the top chunk
A synthesizer on the top chunk; a reader on the full document
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Query-aware assembly matches the context to the intent. A factual question needs only the one or two highest-scoring chunks, and a reader can return the exact span. A summary needs the whole parent section and a generator that can compose across it. A reader cannot summarize, and a synthesizer's extra hops are wasted on a single short chunk.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A team wants to skip retrieval entirely. For each query, it would score every one of five million chunks with a cross-encoder, because the cross-encoder is the most accurate model available. What makes this impractical?
options: Each chunk must be read together with the query, so nothing is precomputed
The cross-encoder cannot bridge the wording gaps that dense retrieval bridges
The cross-encoder needs the chunks embedded with the same model first
The cross-encoder scores are not comparable across different chunks
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: A bi-encoder embeds documents once at indexing time, so a query needs only one embedding and a vector lookup. A cross-encoder reads the query and the candidate together, so every query would need a full model pass over all five million chunks. That is why it is applied only to a shortlist of a few hundred candidates. It handles meaning well, needs no separate embeddings, and its scores are comparable across candidates.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: An agent runs a grounding check only once, on the final answer, just before it is returned to the user. Which failure can this design miss?
options: A bad intermediate result that steers later tool calls off course
A final claim that is not supported by any of the retrieved results
A final answer that drifts away from the user's original question
A final answer that cites a passage the agent never retrieved
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: In an agent loop, the model acts repeatedly, and each observation shapes the next action. A wrong intermediate result can send the following tool calls in the wrong direction. The final answer may then be well grounded in that bad evidence, so a final-only check passes it. The other three failures are exactly what an output check on the final answer catches. Checks should run on each intermediate result and before each action.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: Two RAG systems differ only in their chunking: A uses fixed-size chunks and B uses semantic chunks. On 40 benchmark questions, A answers 30 correctly and B answers 33. B alone is right on 6 questions, and A alone is right on 3. What can the team conclude?
options: No conclusion yet; nine disagreements are too few to rule out chance
B is better; it answers three more questions on the same benchmark
B is better; it wins twice as many disagreements as it loses
No conclusion yet; the 27 questions both got right need a closer look
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Because both systems answered the same questions, only the 9 disagreements carry evidence. If the systems were equally good, each disagreement would be a fair coin toss. A split of 6 to 3 or more uneven, in either direction, then occurs by chance about half the time (p of about 0.51). The questions both systems got right say nothing about which one is better. More questions are needed before the chunking change can be called an improvement.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A fixed pipeline runs query expansion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and a generator. A user asks: "Which firm designed the city's new central library, and who founded that firm?" Why does this pipeline struggle with the question?
options: The second lookup needs the first result, a step the fixed graph lacks
The question is too long for the query expansion stage to rewrite well
The reranker cannot score passages that mention more than one firm
Hybrid retrieval returns parent chunks that are too large for the question
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Finding the founder depends on first learning the firm's name. A fixed pipeline runs one retrieval pass for the whole question, so it cannot chain a follow-up lookup unless someone anticipated that flow and coded it. An agent loop can retrieve the firm first and then use the observed name to look up the founder. Question length, multi-entity passages, and chunk size are not the obstacle.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: A team embeds each 2,000-token manual section as one vector, and questions about a single setting often retrieve the wrong section. Shrinking every chunk to 150 tokens fixes retrieval, but answers now miss steps that appear elsewhere in the same section. Which design resolves both problems?
options: Match on 150-token chunks and pass their parent section to the model
Use 1,000-token chunks everywhere as a compromise between both sizes
Keep 150-token chunks and raise the overlap between them to 100 tokens
Keep 2,000-token sections and rerank them with a cross-encoder
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Retrieval and generation want different chunk sizes. Small chunks embed sharply and match precise questions, while the generator needs the surrounding section to answer completely. Hierarchical chunking keeps both levels: retrieval matches the small chunks, and stored metadata recovers each chunk's parent section for the model. A middle size serves neither job well, more overlap still yields fragments, and reranking cannot sharpen a blurred section embedding at retrieval time.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: For a question about version 3 of a software product, a RAG system retrieves every passage the answer needs. It also retrieves three passages about version 2, which uses similar terms but different settings. What is the main risk?
options: Details from the other version may be mixed into the answer
The generator ignores the extra chunks, since recall is already complete
Faithfulness rises, since more chunks support each claim
Latency rises, but answer quality stays the same
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Context recall is complete, but context precision is low. Irrelevant passages are not harmless padding: they compete for the generator's attention. Closely related but wrong evidence is the most dangerous kind, because it looks relevant, so a version 2 setting can end up in a version 3 answer. Complete recall does not make the model ignore the rest, and wrong-version passages do not support correct claims.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: What does query expansion do in a RAG pipeline?
options: It rewrites or extends the query before retrieval runs
It adds more retrieved passages to the generator's context
It splits long documents into smaller chunks for indexing
It merges the sparse and dense result lists into one ranking
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Query expansion reshapes the raw query so that retrieval can succeed: it fixes spelling, adds synonyms, rewrites the question, or breaks it into sub-questions. It runs before retrieval, so it changes what is searched for, not how many passages reach the generator. Chunking happens at indexing time, and merging result lists is the job of hybrid fusion.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: Compared with a generator that answers from a single retrieval pass, what does a synthesizer gain, and what does it cost?
options: It gains completeness on multi-step questions; it costs latency per hop
It gains exact source wording in answers; it costs fluency in the reply
It gains a lower hallucination risk; it costs the ability to cite sources
It gains shorter prompts per request; it costs recall on simple questions
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: A synthesizer loops: it retrieves, reads, decides what is still missing, and retrieves again. This lets it assemble answers that no single passage contains. Each hop is another round trip through retrieval and reading, so it pays in latency and complexity. It writes rather than copies, so it does not return exact source wording, and it is the hardest form to keep honest, not the safest.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: Which of these is a known weakness of using a language model as a judge of answer quality?
options: It can favour longer answers regardless of their accuracy
It cannot score answers that contain more than one claim
It needs a reference answer for every question it scores
It can only judge answers produced by the same model family
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: An LLM judge is itself a model with blind spots. It can miss subtle factual errors, favour longer answers, and change its verdicts when the evaluation prompt changes, so its scores should be checked against a sample of human judgements. For faithfulness, it splits an answer into claims and checks each one. It can judge without a reference, and it is not tied to one model family.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: Which two answer-quality dimensions can be judged from the question, the answer, and the retrieved context alone, without a reference answer?
options: Faithfulness and answer relevance
Correctness and completeness
Correctness and faithfulness
Completeness and answer relevance
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: Faithfulness checks the answer against the retrieved context, and relevance checks it against the question. Neither needs an expected answer, so both scale to production traffic. Correctness and completeness need a trusted reference that states the right facts. This is why a sound evaluation pairs a small reference set with a larger reference-free sweep.

07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.question: In tool calling, what does the language model itself produce when it decides to use a tool?
options: A structured request naming the tool and its arguments
The tool's result, predicted from its training data
Executable code that the model runs inside its own context
A ranked list of all tools with a score for each one
07 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.explanation: In tool calling, the model emits a structured request that names a tool and its arguments. The surrounding system runs the tool and appends the result to the conversation as the next observation. The model neither executes anything itself nor invents the result, and it picks a tool by name rather than scoring all of them.
